Meaning: In a to the power n, the number a that is being multiplied.
Example: In 2^5, the base is 2.

Meaning: The small raised number saying how many times to multiply the base by itself.
Example: In 2^5, the exponent is 5.

Meaning: A positive whole number: 1, 2, 3, …
Example: n must be a natural number in the definition of a power.

Meaning: a^r · a^s = a^(r+s) and (a^r)^s = a^(rs).
Example: Add the exponents when multiplying; multiply them when taking a power of a power.

Meaning: a^(1/n) is the number which, raised to the power n, gives a.
Example: a^(1/2) is the square root of a.

Meaning: Interest earned on interest. After t years, K(1+p%)^t.
Example: £1,000 at 8% is 1000(1.08)^t after t years.

Meaning: (a+b)² = a²+2ab+b², (a−b)² = a²−2ab+b², (a+b)(a−b) = a²−b².
Example: Learn all three by heart.

Meaning: To multiply out the brackets.
Example: Expand (3x+2y)² to get 9x²+12xy+4y².

Meaning: To write an expression in its shortest equivalent form.
Example: Simplify so the answer contains only positive exponents.

Meaning: The top of a fraction / the bottom of a fraction.
Example: In a/b, a is the numerator and b the denominator.

Meaning: The rate at which a function changes. Written f'(x) or dy/dx.
Example: The derivative measures the slope of the curve at a point.

Meaning: To find the derivative of a function.
Example: Differentiate TR to find MR.

Meaning: How steep a curve is at a point. The derivative gives it.
Example: The MPP is the slope of the TPP curve.

Meaning: Set the first derivative equal to zero: f'(c) = 0. It is NECESSARY for a max or min.
Trap: FOC alone is not enough. It only finds a STATIONARY point.

Meaning: Check the sign of the second derivative to tell a maximum from a minimum.
Example: d²π/dq² = −6 < 0, so q = 33 is a MAXIMUM.
Trap: NEGATIVE second derivative = MAXIMUM. Positive = minimum. Memorise the direction.

Meaning: A point where the function is neither rising nor falling: f'(x) = 0.
Example: A maximum, a minimum or a point of inflection.

Meaning: A point c where f(c) ≥ f(x) for all x in the domain.
Example: At a maximum, dy/dx = 0 and d²y/dx² < 0.

Meaning: A point d where f(d) ≤ f(x) for all x in the domain.
Example: At a minimum, dy/dx = 0 and d²y/dx² > 0.

Meaning: A stationary point that is neither a maximum nor a minimum.
Example: The curve changes the direction it bends.

Meaning: A function that curves downward. Its first derivative is falling.
Example: A concave function has a MAXIMUM.

Meaning: A function that curves upward. Its first derivative is rising.
Example: A convex function has a MINIMUM.

Meaning: To differentiate a function of a function: multiply the outer derivative by the inner one.
Example: Used for composite functions.

Meaning: The rule for differentiating two functions multiplied together.
Example: Integration by parts is the product rule backwards.

Meaning: Finding the input that makes a function as large or as small as possible.
Example: Profit maximisation: find q where dπ/dq = 0.

Meaning: A rule giving one output from each PAIR of inputs, x and y.
Example: F(x,y) uses two inputs to give one output.

Meaning: The derivative with respect to ONE variable, holding the others constant.
Example: Written ∂z/∂x. The curly ∂ means "partial".
Trap: The whole idea: change one variable, FREEZE the rest.

Meaning: Showing which variable is being changed.
Example: ∂z/∂x means the derivative with respect to x.

Meaning: Kept the same while another variable changes.
Example: When y is held constant, z depends only on x.
Trap: This is the mathematical version of IC103's "ceteris paribus".

Meaning: A partial derivative taken a second time.
Example: ∂²f/∂x².

Meaning: A common production function: F(x,y) = Ax^a·y^b.
Example: Used to model how labour and capital produce output.

Meaning: The set of all input values for which a function is defined.
Example: The domain is the set of allowed (x, y) pairs.

Meaning: The reverse of a derivative. It gives the area under a curve.
Example: The definite integral is the area under the graph between a and b.

Meaning: A function whose derivative is the original function.
Example: If F'(x) = f(x), then F is an antiderivative of f.

Meaning: An integral with limits a and b. It gives a NUMBER.
Example: Written ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx.

Meaning: An integral with no limits. It gives a FUNCTION plus a constant C.
Example: Do not forget the + C.
Trap: Definite = a number. Indefinite = a function + C.

Meaning: Links differentiation and integration: the definite integral equals F(b) − F(a).
Example: It is how you actually evaluate a definite integral.

Meaning: The rule for integrating x to a power.
All the values between two end points.
Example: The closed interval [a, b].

Meaning: Able to have a definite integral.
Example: If the area under the graph exists, the function is integrable.

Meaning: A number expressed as a fraction of 100.
The percentage change in value: (New − Old) / Old.
A sequence where each term is the previous one times a constant.
The constant you multiply by in a geometric series. Written k.
Example: In 1, 2, 4, 8 the common ratio is 2.

Term: sum of a finite geometric series
Meaning: sₙ = a(kⁿ − 1)/(k − 1), for k ≠ 1.
Example: Used for annuities and mortgages.

Term: sum of an infinite geometric series
Meaning: s = a/(1 − k), valid only when |k| < 1.
Trap: Only converges when |k| < 1. This is WHY a perpetuity has a finite value.

Meaning: A pound today is worth more than a pound tomorrow, because it can earn interest.
Example: One of the central concepts in finance.
Trap: Same idea as IC101 Lecture 1, now with the algebra behind it.

Meaning: What a future amount is worth today. PV = FV / (1+r)ⁿ.
Example: £2m needed in 2 years at 10% means £1,652,893 today.

Meaning: What an amount today will be worth later. FV = PV(1+r)ⁿ.
Example: £100 at 5% monthly for 12 months gives £179.59.

Meaning: The true annual rate when interest is paid n times a year. R = (1 + r/n)ⁿ − 1.
Example: 5.9% paid quarterly gives 6.03%; 6% paid twice a year gives 6.09%.
Trap: More frequent compounding = a HIGHER effective rate. Classic comparison question.

Meaning: The limit as n goes to infinity: the effective rate becomes e^(rt) − 1.
Example: This is why e appears everywhere in derivatives and bond pricing.

Meaning: The PV of several cash flows is the sum of their separate PVs.
Example: PV(CD1 + CD2) = PV(CD1) + PV(CD2).

Meaning: A stream of fixed cash flows with an INFINITE life. PV = c / r.
Example: A Consol bond, first issued by the UK in 1752. The principal is never repaid.
Trap: PV = c/r. The simplest formula in the module, and it comes from the infinite series.

Meaning: A series of EQUAL cash flows for a FIXED number of periods.
Example: Fixed-rate mortgages and auto loans.
Trap: Annuity = finite. Perpetuity = infinite. That is the only difference.

Example: £250,000 a year for 10 years at 8% is worth £1,677,520 today.

Meaning: The sum of all cash flows discounted to today, including the initial outlay.
Example: Always invest in a project with a positive NPV.

Meaning: The discount rate that makes the NPV of a project exactly ZERO.
Example: Accept the project if IRR > your required rate of return.
Trap: IRR is the rate where NPV = 0. Compare it to the REQUIRED rate to decide.

Meaning: The benchmark return, the discount rate used to compute NPV.
Example: With R = 15% you accept; with R = 30% you reject.

Meaning: A rectangular array of numbers treated as one mathematical object.
Example: A matrix with 4 rows and 3 columns is "of order 4 by 3".
Trap: Written as a BOLD, UPPERCASE letter.

Meaning: The number of rows m and columns n of a matrix.
Example: An m × n matrix.
Trap: ALWAYS rows first, then columns. m × n.

Meaning: One number inside a matrix. aᵢⱼ is in row i, column j.
Example: a₂₃ is in row 2, column 3.

Meaning: A single number, or a 1 × 1 matrix.
Example: Multiplying a matrix by a scalar multiplies every element.

Meaning: A matrix with the same number of rows and columns.
Example: Only square matrices have a determinant or an inverse.

Meaning: The entries aᵢᵢ running from top-left to bottom-right.
Example: All other entries are non-diagonal.

Meaning: A square matrix whose non-diagonal elements are all zero.
Example: Only the diagonal has non-zero numbers.

Meaning: A square matrix with 1s on the diagonal and 0s elsewhere. Written Iₙ.
Example: It behaves like the number 1: AI = A.

Meaning: A square matrix where all entries ABOVE the main diagonal are zero.
A square matrix where all entries BELOW the main diagonal are zero.
A 1 × n matrix: a single row.
Example: Written with a lowercase letter.

Meaning: An n × 1 matrix: a single column.
Example: Written with a lowercase letter.

Meaning: A matrix consisting only of zeros.
Example: It behaves like the number 0.

Meaning: The matrix you get by swapping rows and columns.
Example: Written Aᵀ.

Meaning: A single number computed from a SQUARE matrix.
Example: If the determinant is zero, the matrix has no inverse.
Trap: det = 0 means NO inverse exists. Core exam fact.

Meaning: The matrix A⁻¹ such that A·A⁻¹ = I.
Example: Only square matrices with a non-zero determinant have one.

Meaning: n unknown variables appearing in m linear equations.
Example: Matrices are the tool for solving these.

Meaning: The numbers a₁₁ … aₘₙ multiplying the unknowns.
Example: They form the coefficient matrix.

Meaning: The numbers b₁ … bₘ on the right of the equals signs.
A set of numbers satisfying ALL the equations simultaneously.
Example: s₁, s₂, …, sₙ.

Meaning: A system that has at LEAST one solution.
A system that has NO solution.
Trap: Consistent = has a solution. Inconsistent = none. Easy pair to confuse.
